full_judgment:
2. The case of the petitioner is that he is a former Cabinet Minister and also a former General Secretary of Dhaka University Central Students Union. His wife is a Government servant under the BCS Cadre and was Lecturer in English in the Eden Girls' College on deputation. She was awarded a Full bright Scholarship for prosecution of higher studies in USA. The Government of Bangladesh by its order dated 25.7.91, approved her extra-ordinary leave to prosecute higher studies in USA and thereafter she left for USA in August, 1991. At that time, the petitioner was in detention. His wife left behind their son aged about 7 years to the care of the grandmother of the child. The further ease of the petitioner is that two Criminal Cases being Lalbagh PS Case No. 12(2)91 and Motijheel PS Case No. 55(1)91 were instituted against him by the Government. The former case was instituted under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 for non-compliance of Gazette Notification dated 23.1.91 directing the petitioner to report to the DIG (Prisons) Dhaka for detention the Motijheel PS Case No. 55(1)91 was institued under sections 409/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. 1947 against several persons including the present petitioner alleging that the present petitioner presided over a meeting of the Board of Directors, Bangladesh Biman on 16.3.89 and 6.7.89 when the decision regarding purchase of three ATP Aircrafts were approved which caused loss to the State. 

 3. The petitioner preferred Miscellaneous case Nos. 578 and 579 of 1991 before the High Court Division for bail and bail was granted to the petitioner in both the cases. Thereafter, the petitioner instituted Criminal Revision Nos. 978 of 1991 and 435 of 1992 in this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceeding of the aforesaid two criminal cases. Both these revision cases are still pending before this Court. 

 4. The further case of the petitioner is, that after his release on bail, his minor son has been staying with him and he along with his son intended to make a short visit to his wife in USA and for that purpose he applied to the respondents for an International Passport being application No.19676/92 dated 15.5.91 on payment of requisite fees. The respondent No. 3 by the impugned Memo. Annexure-'A' informed the petitioner about the inability of the government to issue any Passport to the petitioner. The petitioner, being the citizen of Bangladesh, has a right guaranteed under the Constitution to travel in and outside of the country. The respondents in an arbitrary manner without conveying the reasons of non-issuance of passport and without giving an opportunity of hearing him, refused to issue passport to him. The order is malafide and has been passed at the behest of the interested persons without application of mind. The impugned order is absolutely void being violative of the principles of natural justice and also of Articles 27, 31, 32, and 36 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 5. The respondent No. 1 entered appearance by filing an affidavit-in-opposition through Mr. Altafur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General denying the material allegations contained in the petition. The respondent claims that two Criminal Cases being Lalbagh PS Case No. 12(2)94 and Motijheel PS Case No. 55(1)91 were instituted against the petitioner. The authority apprehended that the petitioner, to evade prosecution in the above two cases may leave the country if a passport is issued to him. So, the Government has decided not to issue any passport in order to prevent him from going out of the country. The respondent further claims that the reasons of non-issuance of the passport to the petitioner was conveyed to the petitioner on 11.2.93 upon a demand notice received from the petitioner. Thus, according to the respondent, the allegation of the petitioner to the effect that the reasons of non-issuance of the passport was not conveyed to him is not true. The respondent also claimed that the decision of the respondents regarding non-issuance of the passport to the petitioner is neither malafide nor illegal since it aimed at vindicating public interest. The decision also did not violate any provision of the Constitution. 

 6. Annexure-A is the impugned Memo. From this Memo, it appears that with reference to the application for issuance of an International Passport to the petitioner, an Assistant Director of Regional Passport Office, Dhaka Informed the petitioner about the inability of the Government to issue any passport to him. We find that no reasons as to the inability of the Government have been mentioned in this Memo. Under the provision of Article 4(2) of the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973 power has been given to the authority for refusal to issue passport or travel document to an applicant. It appears that the passport authority is required to make such enquiry as it may consider necessary on receipt of an application for issuance of passport and subject to the provision of this Order, the authority may by order in writing refuse to issue passport to an applicant. It is true that there is no provision for issuance of any notice to an applicant in case of refusal to issue a passport on the basis of his application. But from the judicial pronouncements of this court and the Superior Courts of the Sub-continent it has been settled that either in case of cancellation or refusal of issuance of passport to a citizen, an opportunity should be given to the person concerned to show cause against the grounds of his being so debarred. In this connection, the learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to the case of Syed Mokbul Hossain vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR 39. From this case it appears that the facts of the case relate to revocation of passport. However, it appears that the Court while discussing question of revocation or cancellation of passport also discussed the question of refusal to grant passport. After taking into consideration the several decisions of the Indian Supreme Court and the Pakistan Supreme Court, the Court was pleased to hold that while exercising the power of refusing to grant or impounding or cancelling a passport, the authority would do well to remember that it is a basic human right recognized in Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights with which passport authority is interfering, when it ref uses or impounds or cancels a passport. It is a highly valuable right which is a part of personal liberty, an aspect of the spiritual dimension of man, and it should not be lightly interfered with. 

 7. The learned Advocate rot the petitioner also referred to an unreported case, the judgment of which was delivered on 27.2.1994 in Writ Petition No.1073 of 1993 in the case of Begum Monsura Rahman Mohiuddin vs. Government of Bangladesh and others. Facts of this case are similar to the facts of the present case. In this case, the petitioner's prayer for issuing a passport was rejected by the Government. It further appears that in that case the Government ref used to issue passport on the ground of pendency or a criminal case against the petitioner. The Court, after discussing the facts relating to the criminal case was pleased to hold that there was no material to show that the petitioner might evade prosecution if passport is issued in her favour. 

 8. In the case before us, while refusing to issue passport by the Memo. Annexure-A, the petitioner was not informed of the reasons of non-issuance of passport. However, in the affidavit-in-opposition, the respondent claimed that the reasons of non-issuance of passport, was conveyed to the petitioner after receipt or the demand notice on 11.2.93. No copy of that communication has been filed along with the affidavit-in-opposition. So, this Court is not in a position to know as to what were the reasons for non-issuance of the passport to the petitioner. However, it has been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner may leave the country to evade prosecution which were pending against him if passport is issued to him. Admittedly, two criminal cases being Lalbagh PS Case No. 12(2) 91 and Motijheel PS case No. 55(1)91 were started against the petitioner. The petitioner was granted bail by this Court in Criminal Misc. Case Nos. 578 and 579 of 1991. It further appears that the petitioner already filed two criminal revisions being Criminal Revision Nos. 978 of 1991 and 435 of 1992 in this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings of the aforesaid two criminal cases. These two criminal revision cases are still pending for disposal. From the materials brought before us we find nothing to show and to believe that the petitioner might evade prosecution if passport is issued to him. 

 9. From the statements made in the affidavit- in-opposition it is clear that the reasons for non-issuance of passport to the petitioner was not conveyed to him before taking the decisions. The respondent claims that the reasons were conveyed on 11.2.93 and it was received by the representative of the petitioner on 26.2.93. From the record it appears that the Rule was issued on 31.1.93 and it was received by the respondents on 15.2.93. So it is clean that if at all the reasons were communicated to the petitioner, it was done after receipt of the Rule by the respondents. In any case, the fact remains that the petitioner was not given any opportunity to explain his position before his prayer for issuance of passport was refused. The power conferred under Article 5(2) of the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973 regarding refusal to issue passport should be exercised judiciously. The right of a citizen to leave and re-enter Bangladesh has been guaranteed under Article 36 of the Constitution. Before this right is curtailed and a citizen is debarred from enjoying this right, natural justice demands that he should be given an opportunity to place his views as to the reasons for non-issuance of passport to him. From Article 6 of the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973, we find that passport authority is empowered to refuse to issue any passport to a citizen on several grounds as stated in that Article itself. In the present case, the petitioner was not informed of the grounds as to why his prayer for issuing passport was refused nor he was given any opportunity to be heard. In view of the above discussions, we are of the opinion that the impugned Memo refusing the petitioner's prayer to issue passport to him has been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.
